hello.note: Respectful, often with palms pressed together. Friends usually just say 'hai'.

goodbye.note: Lit. 'I'll go and come back', said by the one leaving; a bare 'I'm going' sounds final.

please.note: Formal. In speech politeness usually comes from the ending -amo? ('could you?'), e.g. tharamo?

thank_you.note: Spelled nandi but said nanni. Thank you very much: valare nanni (വളരെ നന്ദി).

youre_welcome.note: Lit. 'What of it?', i.e. it was nothing. There is no set reply; saramilla ('it's nothing') is also common.

yes.note: Casual: um (ഉം). A sideways tilt of the head also means yes or OK.

no.note: To turn down something offered, say venda (വേണ്ട, 'I don't want it').

sorry.note: For small slips, the English 'sorry' is very common in everyday speech.

excuse_me.note: To a woman: ചേച്ചീ, ഒന്നു ചോദിച്ചോട്ടെ? (chechee, onnu chodichotte?). Chetta/chechi = elder brother/sister.

good_morning.note: Formal, heard on radio and TV. Face to face, most people say 'good morning' in English.

how_are_you.note: Friendly, to someone you know: enthokkeyundu vishesham? ('What's new?')

im_fine.note: Often just sukham. To ask back: ningalkko? ('And you?')

whats_your_name.note: Very formal: thankalude instead of ningalude. Casual: perentha?

where_from.note: Between Malayalis the usual question is nadu evideya? ('Where's your home town?')

im_from.note: Nadu means home country or home town. This pattern needs no case ending on the place name.

speak_english.note: Lit. 'Do you know English?', the usual way to ask.

speak_slowly.note: The ending -amo? ('could you?') makes it a polite request. Pathukke also means 'softly'.

why.note: In speech often enthina? ('what for?') or enthe?

who.note: In speech usually ആരാ? (ara?), e.g. at the door: 'Who is it?'

how_much.note: Also: ithinu entha vila? ('What's its price?')

where_bathroom.note: 'Toilet' (ടോയ്‌ലറ്റ്) is just as common. Public signs may say ശൗചാലയം.

can_you_help.note: Onnu ('just a bit') softens a request.

one.note: Before a noun it becomes oru: oru chaya (one tea). Old Malayalam digit: ൧.

two.note: Malayalam digit: ൨ (rarely used today; 2 is standard).

seven.note: zh is ഴ, said with the tongue curled back, somewhere between r and l. Digit: ൭

ten.note: The old sign for ten is ൰; today it is written 10.

water.note: Cold water: thanuttha vellam. Eateries often serve warm herbal water by default.

tea.note: Comes with milk and sugar; black tea is kattan chaya (കട്ടൻ ചായ).

bread.note: Means loaf bread; 'bread' (ബ്രെഡ്) is also common. Flatbreads have their own names: chapathi, porotta.

menu_please.note: Small eateries may have no menu: ask enthokke undu? ('What is there?')

bill_please.note: Also common: ethrayayi? ('How much has it come to?')

no_meat.note: Fish and egg don't count as irachi. To rule them out too: njan vejitteriyan anu.

enjoy_meal.note: There is no set 'bon appétit'; hosts urge guests to eat like this. Lit. 'Eat well!'

left.note: To a driver: idatthottu (ഇടത്തോട്ട്, 'to the left').

right.note: To a driver: valatthottu (വലത്തോട്ട്, 'to the right').

stop_here.note: Lit. 'Stopping here is enough', the usual line to taxi and auto drivers.

airport.note: In everyday speech most people say eyarporttu (എയർപോർട്ട്).

hotel.note: In Kerala hottal often means a restaurant; for a place to stay people also say lodge or 'room'.

want_to_go.note: Vare means 'as far as'; it works with any place name, no case ending needed.

is_it_far.note: Can I walk there?: nadannu pokan pattumo?

one_ticket.note: On a bus, just tell the conductor the stop and the number, e.g. 'Aluva, onnu'.

cheaper.note: To bargain: kurachu kuraykkamo? ('Can you bring it down a bit?')

id_like_this.note: Lit. 'This will do for me.' Also: ithu edukkam ('I'll take this').

pay_card.note: Lit. 'Do you take card?' Phone payments are more common: UPI undo?

cash.note: I'll pay cash: kashayi tharam. Formal word: panam (പണം).

open.note: Shop signs are mostly in English. To ask: thurannittundo? ('Is it open?')

big.note: On its own ('a big one'): valuthu (വലുത്).

small.note: On its own ('a small one'): cheruthu (ചെറുത്).

yesterday.note: Keep them apart: innu (today), innale (yesterday), nale (tomorrow).

now.note: In speech: ippo. Right now: ippo thanne.

good_evening.note: Formal. In person most people say namaskaram or 'good evening'.

good_night.note: Formal. Family and friends usually say 'good night' in English.

wait_moment.note: Very common in speech: oru minute! The -e ending makes it a gentle request.

help.note: Ayyo! is the all-purpose cry of alarm and will also bring people running.

im_lost.note: Lit. 'The way went wrong for me.'

dont_feel_well.note: Also very common: enikku vayya (എനിക്ക് വയ്യ, 'I'm not up to it').

allergic.note: The item goes in unchanged, e.g. enikku podi alarjiyanu (dust).

no_problem.note: Also: saramilla ('never mind'), the usual reply to an apology.

i_like_it.note: On first trying something: enikku ishtamayi ('I've taken to it').

dont_like_it.note: Softer: athra ishtamayilla ('I didn't like it much').

im_happy.note: Enikku ('to me') phrases stay the same whether a man or a woman says them.

welcome.note: Swagatham (സ്വാഗതം) is for signs and speeches; at the door hosts say this.

my_family.note: Warmer and very common: ente veettukar (എന്റെ വീട്ടുകാർ, 'my people at home').

mother.note: Many Muslim families say umma (ഉമ്മ). Formal: mathavu (മാതാവ്).

father.note: Many Christian families say appan or pappa; many Muslim families say uppa or vappa.

brother.note: Formal. In speech people say which: chettan (ചേട്ടൻ, elder) or aniyan (അനിയൻ, younger).

sister.note: Formal. In speech people say which: chechi (ചേച്ചി, elder) or aniyatthi (അനിയത്തി, younger).

child.note: This is 'son'; daughter: മകൾ (makal). Children (plural): makkal (മക്കൾ).

friend.note: Female friend: കൂട്ടുകാരി (koottukari). Suhrutthu (സുഹൃത്ത്) fits both but is formal.

this_is_my_friend.note: For a woman friend: ഇത് എന്റെ കൂട്ടുകാരിയാണ് (ithu ente koottukariyanu).

are_you_married.note: Lit. 'Has your wedding happened?' Formal: vivahithanano? (to a man), vivahithayano? (to a woman).

have_children.note: Kuttikal undo? ('Any kids?') is just as common.

monday.note: Every day name ends in -azhcha. No word for 'on' is needed: thinkalazhcha kanam (see you Monday).

thursday.note: Two zh sounds (ഴ): curl the tongue back for both.

sunday.note: Starts with nj (ഞ), like the ny in 'canyon'.

weekend.note: Formal. In speech: 'weekend' (വീക്കെൻഡ്) or shaniyum njayarum ('Saturday and Sunday').

what_day.note: For the date ask: innu ethram theeyathiyanu? (ഇന്ന് എത്രാം തീയതിയാണ്?)

eleven.note: Most of 11–18 are pathi(n)- ('ten') + the unit, but 12 is panthrandu and 19 patthombathu. Digits: ൧൧

twenty.note: Add units with -tth-: irupatthonnu (ഇരുപത്തൊന്ന്, 21). Malayalam digits: ൨൦

hundred.note: No 'one' needed. The old sign for 100 is ൱; today it is written 100.

thousand.note: No 'one' needed: ayiram roopa (1,000 rupees). The old sign for 1000 is ൲.

how_old.note: More formal: ningalude prayam ethrayanu? (നിങ്ങളുടെ പ്രായം എത്രയാണ്?)

years_old.note: The number goes in unchanged, e.g. enikku muppathu vayassayi. Also: enikku … vayassundu.

red.note: Before a noun: chuvanna (ചുവന്ന), e.g. chuvanna kuda (a red umbrella).

green.note: Also means raw or unripe: pacha manga (raw mango).

white.note: Before a noun: veluttha (വെളുത്ത). Don't mix it up with vellam (water).

this_one.note: To ask for it: ithu tharamo? ('Could you give me this?')

that_one.note: Further off: avideyullathu (അവിടെയുള്ളത്, 'the one over there').

another_one.note: For drinks or dishes, name it: oru chaya koodi (one more tea).

its_hot.note: Nalla … undu ('there's a good deal of …') is the usual weather pattern. Casual: enthoru choodu!

its_raining.note: Heavy rain: nalla mazha. The monsoon season: mazhakkalam (മഴക്കാലം).

weather_today.note: Small talk usually goes straight to rain: innu mazha peyyumo? ('Will it rain today?')

beautiful_day.note: Thelinja = clear, bright. Nalla divasam alone can mean an auspicious day.

summer.note: Often just venal (വേനൽ). Kalam means season.

winter.note: Lit. 'mist season', Kerala's cool months. Formal: shaithyakalam (ശൈത്യകാലം).

have_reservation.note: Lit. 'I have booked a room.' Then give the name: … enna perilanu ('under the name …').

wifi_password.note: Wi-Fi is said vaifai. Shorter: pasvedu entha?

check_out_time.note: Ethra manikku = 'at what o'clock'. A reply: pathinonnu manikku (at eleven).

map.note: Formal: bhoopadam (ഭൂപടം). Mappu also means 'pardon'; context makes it clear.

bus.note: The main bus station is called the 'bus stand' (ബസ് സ്റ്റാൻഡ്).

is_this_seat_free.note: Lit. 'Is anyone on this seat?' Usual reply: illa, irunnoloo ('No, have a seat').

i_work_in.note: Add -il ('in') to the place: njan bankil joli cheyyunnu (in a bank).

im_student.note: A woman says: ഞാൻ ഒരു വിദ്യാർത്ഥിനിയാണ് (njan oru vidyarthiniyanu). Casual: njan padikkuvanu.

meeting.note: Formal: yogam (യോഗം), for official or public meetings.

im_busy.note: Thirakku also means a crowd or rush.

day_off.note: Today's my day off: innu enikku avadhiyanu. 'Leave' (ലീവ്) is common too.

colleague.note: Female: സഹപ്രവർത്തക (sahapravartthaka). In speech 'colleague' (കൊളീഗ്) is common.

lets_start.note: Namukku is 'we' including the listener. Casual: thudangiyalo? ('Shall we start?')

good_job.note: Casual: kollam! ('nice!') or kalakki! ('you nailed it!')

table_for_two.note: Kittumo? ('can I get?') is a handy polite way to ask for anything.

what_recommend.note: Lit. 'What's special here?' Or: ethanu nallathu? ('Which is good?')

not_spicy.note: Just a little: erivu kurachu mathi. Chilli heat is erivu; choodu is temperature.

vegetarian_food.note: Usually just 'veg': veg undo? Formal: sasyaharam (സസ്യാഹാരം).

no_sugar.note: At tea shops just say 'without': oru chaya without (ഒരു ചായ വിത്തൗട്ട്).

im_full.note: To stop a host serving more: mathi! ('enough!')

takeaway.note: In Kerala 'parcel' is the word for takeaway. To ask if they do it: parsal undo?

keep_change.note: Bakki (ബാക്കി) is the change, lit. 'the rest'.

head_hurts.note: Lit. 'I have head-pain.' Vedana (pain) works with any body part.

have_fever.note: A cold: jaladosham (ജലദോഷം). A cough: chuma (ചുമ).

medicine.note: You 'eat' medicine: marunnu kazhikkuka (to take medicine).

call_ambulance.note: Emergency number in India: 112. In Kerala the ambulance line is 108.

need_rest.note: Casual: kurachu rest edukkanam ('I need to take some rest').

feel_better.note: Also very common: ippo kuravundu ('it has eased now').

lets_meet.note: Among friends: namukku onnu koodam ('let's get together').

are_you_free.note: Lit. 'Do you have time tomorrow?' Casual: nale free ano?

call_me.note: Vilikkuka means both 'call out to' and 'phone'. Onnu and the -e ending make it a gentle request.

your_number.note: Often: nambar onnu tharamo? ('Could you give me your number?')

see_you_soon.note: The everyday goodbye is pinne kanam ('see you later').

have_nice_day.note: Formal, mostly in messages. In person people say 'have a nice day' in English.

good_luck.note: Lit. 'All good wishes!' In speech, 'all the best!' in English is the usual wish.

happy_birthday.note: Formal: janmadinashamsakal (ജന്മദിനാശംസകൾ). Many just say 'happy birthday'.

miss_you.note: Ninne (you) is for friends and younger family. More native: ninne kanan thonnunnu ('I long to see you').
